study.title: John 10 The door, the good shepherd and the security of the flock
study.overview: John 10 presents Jesus as the true shepherd in contrast to false leaders, mercenaries and thieves. The image of the flock shows that the true people of God recognize the voice of Christ, follow him and find in him life, protection and pasture. The chapter also reveals that the identity of Jesus is not only that of a moral guide: it presents itself as the door of access to salvation, the good shepherd who gives his own life for the sheep, and the one whose unity with the Father provokes division, rejection and, at the same time, faith. The outcome shows that, outside the religious center of Jerusalem, many believe in it.

outline.title: The figure of the fold and the known voice
outline.explanation: Jesus describes the contrast between the intruder and the legitimate pastor. The sheep recognize the voice of the shepherd, are called individually and follow him, while fleeing the stranger. The text shows that the parable was not immediately understood by the listeners.

outline.title: Jesus is the door and the good shepherd
outline.explanation: Jesus explains the image: he himself is the gateway to salvation and to the support of the flock. He denounces the thief, claims to give life in abundance and presents himself as the good shepherd who delivers his life for the sheep. He also speaks of other sheep, announcing a single flock under one shepherd.

outline.title: Division, accusation and unity with the Father
outline.explanation: The words of Jesus divide the Jews: some accuse him of being demon-possessed; others argue that his works do not match such an accusation. At the feast of the renewal of the Temple, Jesus states that his works testify of him, declares that his sheep belong to him and conclude that he and the Father are one. The reaction is of accusation of blasphemy and attempted imprisonment.

outline.title: Withdrawal beyond the Jordan and renewed faith
outline.explanation: Jesus goes to the other side of the Jordan, to the place where John baptized, and there many recognize the truth of John's testimony about him. The chapter ends with the note that many believed in Jesus in that place.

study.context: The provided notes are an important part of the chapter at the feast of Temple renewal in Jerusalem in winter. This context helps to understand the confrontation with the Jewish leaders in the temple, especially at the entrance of Solomon. The notes also highlight that the image of the shepherd and the sheep is based on the tradition of the Old Testament, where God is the shepherd of Israel and where spiritual leaders are assessed as pastors of the people. Another important observation is that Jesus withdraws to the place where John baptized, and there he finds faith greater than in the holy city.
study.theology: The chapter teaches, first of all, that salvation is not found by religious shortcuts or self-proclaimed leadership, but by entering into Christ, the door. Secondly, Jesus not only guides the flock: he guards him with his own life. The good shepherd does not abandon the sheep in the face of danger; on the contrary, he surrenders himself for them. Thirdly, the security of those who belong to Christ is presented as the work of Christ himself and of the Father: no one can anchor them from the hand of the Son or from the hand of the Father. This does not eliminate the need to listen and follow the voice of Jesus, but shows that the perseverance of the flock depends on the power of God, not of human fragility. Fourthly, unity between the Son and the Father is not a secondary detail, but a central part of the identity of Jesus; therefore his works and his words demand faith. The chapter also points to the inclusion of other sheep, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd. The faith of the last verses shows that John's testimony and the works of Jesus converge to lead people to believe in him.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter resumes the biblical tradition of the pastor of Israel and applies this image to Jesus, in contrast to leaders who do not take good care of the flock.
There is division between listeners because the words of Christ become a cause for confrontation; it is better that people divide about their doctrine than they remain united in opposition to it.
The Oother sheep are understood as the Gentiles and Samaritans, who would also be gathered in one flock under one shepherd.

questions: Does my life show that I recognize the voice of Christ above other religious, cultural or personal voices?
Have I sought security in Christ as the door of salvation and the good shepherd, or in human leadership, self-performance and external structures?
How can I participate in the care of the flock of Christ without acting as a mercenary, but with love, fidelity and sacrifice?
study.practice: This week, read the chapter slowly and write down where the actions of Jesus appear: call, lead, give life, keep, know, give life and gather. Then examine whether your faith is more supported by external signs or in the voice of Christ. Practice concrete obedience to a clear order of Jesus in the gospels, as a way of responding to the Shepherd who calls his sheep by name. If you serve in leadership, do so with real pastoral zeal, avoiding seeking gain of one's own and learning to remain when the cost comes.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text provided does not explain in detail who are exactly all interlocutors at each moment, nor does it allow to determine with absolute certainty the chronological sequence in relation to the previous chapter. The notes also do not authorize precise dates or geographical identifications beyond what is explicitly said, so the study avoids broader historical conjectures.
